notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes, compiled from what the searched pages actually say.

---

## Deuteronomy 4:25-49 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

---

### v. 25: *"After you have children and grandchildren and you have been in the land a long time, if you then act corruptly and make an idol of any form—doing evil in the sight of the LORD your God and provoking Him to anger—"*

**Traditional Reading:**

Moses now speaks as a prophet, foretelling the future apostasy of Israel. The Pulpit Commentary notes that Moses predicts the evil that would come "when in after years a generation should arise that had not known the things they had seen, or had forgotten them (ver. 9), and the nation should then become wanton and corrupt, and fall into idolatry." The phrase "remained long in the land" literally means "have become old, an ancient nation." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/4.htm)

Ellicott makes a vivid observation: the Hebrew literally suggests "shall slumber"—"a very suggestive expression. Prosperity often sends true religion to sleep, and brings conventional, or fashionable, religion in its stead." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/4.htm)

Gill traces the timeline: "during the times of the judges, they were in their childhood, or youth; in the times of David and Solomon, they were in their manhood; after that, in their decline; and in the times of Jeconiah and his brethren in their old age, when for their sins they were carried captive." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/4.htm)

Keil & Delitzsch add: "'Growing old in the land' involved forgetfulness of the former manifestations of grace on the part of the Lord, but not necessarily becoming voluptuous through the enjoyment of the riches of the land." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/4-25.htm)

The Cambridge Bible notes the verb "corrupt yourselves" (shachath) — the same verb used of the morally rotten state of the world in Genesis 6:11-12. The "corrupting agent" is idolatry. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/4-25.htm)

Precept Austin emphasizes that God says "when" not "if" — the Omniscient God sees the future failure of His people. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy_425-31_commentary)

**Where Traditions Differ:**

No major Protestant tradition disputes the basic reading. The difference lies in what follows: dispensational interpreters (MacArthur, Precept Austin) see this as a prophecy fulfilled progressively through Assyrian (722 BC), Babylonian (586 BC), and Roman (AD 70) exiles, with the ultimate restoration still future. Amillennial or covenant theologians may see it as fulfilled in the Babylonian exile with spiritual application to the church.

---

### v. 26: *"I call heaven and earth as witnesses against you this day that you will quickly perish from the land that you are crossing the Jordan to possess. You will not live long upon it, but will be utterly destroyed."*

**Traditional Reading:**

The Pulpit Commentary: "Moses speaks in the name of the Lord of all, and so calls to witness the whole created universe to attest his words; the heavens and earth are witnesses for God, and when evil comes on those who transgress his Law, they declare his righteousness (Psalm 50:4, 6)." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/4.htm)

Keil & Delitzsch clarify: "Heaven and earth do not stand here for the rational beings dwelling in them, but are personified, represented as living, and capable of sensation and speech, and mentioned as witnesses who would raise up against Israel … to bear witness that God … had warned the people." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/4-25.htm)

Precept Austin cites the KJV Bible Commentary that this "is in the accusative case, which means to give a witness against a person under oath." Bob Utley adds that calling heaven and earth as witnesses "was part of the Suzerain Hittite Treaties" and "reflects the Israeli legal system's need for two witnesses in a court case (cf. Deut. 17:6; 19:15)." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy_425-31_commentary)

Enduring Word (David Guzik): "creation itself would testify against them." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-4/)

---

### v. 27: *"Then the LORD will scatter you among the peoples, and only a few of you will survive among the nations to which the LORD will drive you."*

**Traditional Reading:**

This is a clear prophecy of the diaspora. Precept Austin records: "This prophecy was first fulfilled when the 10 northern tribes were carried into exile in Assyria in 722 BC (2 Kings 17:6) and the 2 Southern tribes, Judah and Benjamin, were taken into exile in Babylon in 586 BC (2 Chr 36:15-21). In addition, the nation of Israel was scattered from her land after her rejection of Christ, this dispersion occurring at the hands of the Romans." The Hebrew verb for "scatter" is translated in the Septuagint with *diaspeiro*, calling to mind the Jewish diaspora. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy_425-31_commentary)

The Pulpit Commentary observes: "From Leviticus 26:33, etc., and Deuteronomy 28:64, it is evident that the author had in view 'all the dispersions which would come upon the rebellious nation in future times, even down to the dispersion under the Romans, which continues still; so that Moses contemplated the punishment in its fullest extent' (Keil)." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/4.htm)

**Where Traditions Differ:**

Dispensational teachers (MacArthur, cited by Precept Austin) emphasise that though Jews returned under Ezra and Nehemiah, "they never regained their autonomy or dominance. Thus, the days of promised restoration and return look forward to Messiah's return to set up the millennial kingdom." This is a distinctively dispensational, futurist reading. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy_425-31_commentary)

---

### v. 28: *"And there you will serve man-made gods of wood and stone, which cannot see or hear or eat or smell."*

**Traditional Reading:**

Gill notes the irony: the Jews, who were set free from Egyptian bondage to serve Jehovah, would instead serve dumb idols. Precept Austin calls this "GOTTA SERVE SOMEBODY! GOD OR IDOLS" and cites Bob Dylan's classic line: "It may be the devil or it may be the Lord, but you gotta serve somebody!" The commentary adds: "If man does not serve God, he will by default serve gods!" (https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy_425-31_commentary)

Enduring Word: "If Israel was scattered in exile, they would then get their fill of idols. God would put them in places filled with idols." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-4/)

The polemic against idols—"which neither see nor hear nor eat nor smell"—is a recurring theme in Scripture (cf. Psalm 115:4-7; Isaiah 44:9-20), highlighting the utter futility of idol worship.

---

### v. 29: *"But if from there you will seek the LORD your God, you will find Him if you seek Him with all your heart and with all your soul."*

**Traditional Reading:**

Precept Austin calls this "A BLESSED 'BUT'!" — comparing it to the great "but God" of Ephesians 2:4. The note says: "No man, Jew or Gentile, seeks for God (Rom 3:11, Ps 14:2), so in order for the dispersed Jews in the latter days to seek for Him, God Himself (His Spirit) must put that desire in their heart. Of course, they still have the responsibility to follow through and 'seek for Him' — this is a great mystery — God's sovereign provision, man's responsibility." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy_425-31_commentary)

Enduring Word quotes Thompson: "'Even in the predicament of exile God may be sought and found. One feature of Yahweh's covenant with Israel in contrast with the secular treaties was that a rebel might return ('repent') to Yahweh and be forgiven and thus have the prospect of beginning a new life of obedience.'" Guzik adds: "to seek God with the heart has the idea of passionately seeking Him, seeking Him out of true commitment and devotion to the LORD. Seeking God with the soul has the idea of seeking God with the mind, will, and emotions; the surrender of one's whole being to God." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-4/)

**Baptist View (Spurgeon):**

C.H. Spurgeon preached two sermons on these verses: "Conversions Encouraged" and "Earnest Seeking Successful." He applies the text universally: "The Lord, here, encourages sinners to turn to Himself and find abundant Grace. He encourages sinners who had violated His plainest commandments, who had made idols and so had corrupted themselves—and had, consequently, been visited with captivity and other chastisements—He invites them to turn from their evil ways and seek His face." Yet he notes that "if the text has any limited aspect, if it is to be regarded as uttered to any special character among transgressors, it peculiarly belongs to backsliders, for the people to whom it was first addressed were the people of God." Spurgeon emphasizes: "We have not, then, to bring anything to God, but to seek Him. We have not to seek a righteousness to bring to Him, nor seek a state of heart which will fit us for Him, but to seek Him at once!" (https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/conversions-encouraged)

**Reformed View:**

Calvin does not treat this verse separately in the material retrieved, but the Precept Austin site's emphasis on God's sovereign initiation of the seeking (citing Romans 3:11) reflects a Reformed understanding of divine sovereignty in salvation. The Ligonier/Gospel Coalition material frames the future hope as predicated "on the merciful initiative of God." (https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/deuteronomy/)

---

### v. 30: *"When you are in distress and all these things have happened to you, then in later days you will return to the LORD your God and listen to His voice."*

**Traditional Reading:**

Precept Austin devotes extensive space to this verse's eschatological significance. The time phrase "in the latter days" is key. The distress (Hebrew *tsar*; Septuagint *thlipsis*) is linked to the "Great Tribulation" of Matthew 24:21, the "time of Jacob's trouble" (Jeremiah 30:7). The commentary traces a chain of prophecies: Daniel 12:1, Zechariah 12:10, Romans 11:26-27, concluding that "in the last days prior to (and including) the return of Israel's Messiah, Israel will undergo a time of distress … So the reason these Jews in the latter days will mourn is because they have been given the Spirit of grace." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy_425-31_commentary)

Matthew Henry's Concise Commentary: "Afflictions engage and quicken us to seek God; and, by the grace of God working with them, many are thus brought back to their right mind." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/4-25.htm)

**Where Traditions Differ:**

The dispensational, futurist reading (Precept Austin, MacArthur) sees the "latter days" as specifically the end-times tribulation and Israel's national conversion prior to the millennium. Amillennial Reformed interpreters (e.g., Gospel Coalition) tend to see the restoration promises as fulfilled in Christ and the church, without a distinct future for national Israel. The Cambridge Bible notes that some critical scholars consider vv. 29-31 a "later exilic insertion" — though this is not a traditional Protestant view. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/4-25.htm)

---

### v. 31: *"For the LORD your God is a merciful God; He will not abandon you or destroy you or forget the covenant with your fathers, which He swore to them by oath."*

**Traditional Reading:**

Precept Austin identifies "the covenant with your fathers" not as the conditional Mosaic Covenant but "the unconditional promises of the Abrahamic Covenant … made first with Abraham and then reaffirmed both to Isaac and then to Jacob." MacArthur is quoted: "God mercifully, not because they deserve it, will fulfill the covenant He made with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob with repentant Israel in the future. God will not forget the Word that He has given to Abraham and his seed (cf. Rom 11:25–27)." The ESV Study Bible note adds: "In Deuteronomy, mercy is grounded in the Lord's faithfulness to the Abrahamic promises (Dt 9:27; 30:5, 20). God will maintain his covenant with Abraham, even if Israel forgets it (4:23; see Rom. 3:3–4)." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy_425-31_commentary)

The Nelson Study Bible: "The future of God's people depends on God's love. The emphasis on God's mercy in this verse is a necessary balance to the emphasis that Moses placed on God's refining wrath (Dt 4:24)." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy_425-31_commentary)

Dummelow: "Such repentance procures the divine mercy, for God does not forget His part of the covenant, however His people forget theirs. 'The gifts and calling of God are without repentance,' i.e. they are irrevocable: see Romans 11:29; Hebrews 6:17." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/deuteronomy-4.html)

Spurgeon's sermon highlights three encouragements from this text: "'For the Lord thy God is a merciful God; He will not forsake thee.' Catch at that, sinner … 'Neither destroy thee.' You have been afraid He would … but the Lord will not destroy you … 'Thou shalt find Him if thou seek Him.' What more, poor sinner, what more dost thou want?" (https://biblehub.com/sermons/deuteronomy/4-29.htm)

---

### v. 32: *"Indeed, ask now from one end of the heavens to the other about the days that long preceded you, from the day that God created man on earth: Has anything as great as this ever happened or been reported?"*

**Traditional Reading:**

Calvin: "Moses here more forcibly extols and pronounces magnificent praises upon the miracles … his object being to produce a fuller conviction of its dignity. He magnifies, too, by comparison, the testimonies whereby its authority had been ratified, viz., because nothing like it had ever occurred; for if any such instance had previously taken place, some portion of its preciousness or honor would have been taken from it. But since from the beginning of the world only one such illustrious manifestation of His power had been given by God, it afforded the greater sanction to the Law." Calvin rejects the "more refined exposition" that heaven and earth are witnesses here, preferring the simple sense that Moses "desires them to inquire and to examine whether from the creation of the world, or in any most remote region, any such thing had come to pass." (https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/comment3/comm_vol03/htm/v.viii.htm)

Enduring Word: "Moses asked Israel to carefully think about the days that are past and consider if God had ever dealt with any other nation the way He had dealt with Israel. Israel had a specially blessed place in the plan of God." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-4/)

Constable: "The passage at hand is without comparison as a discourse on the doctrine of God." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/deuteronomy-4.html)

---

### v. 33: *"Has a people ever heard the voice of God speaking out of the fire, as you have, and lived?"*

**Traditional Reading:**

Calvin emphasizes the uniqueness: "It is true, indeed, that the superstitions of the Gentiles had been confirmed of old by many apparitions, yet amongst the portents which wretched men have imagined for their willing self-deception, there is nothing approaching to this miracle. Many have individually lied, and their false and foolish tales have been rashly believed; but here we have not to do with unfounded and scattered rumors, nor with the dreams of some single person, but Moses produces more than 700,000 witnesses, to whom God's glory had clearly and certainly appeared." (https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/comment3/comm_vol03/htm/v.viii.htm)

---

### v. 34: *"Or has any god tried to take as his own a nation out of another nation—by trials, signs, wonders, and war, by a strong hand and an outstretched arm, and by great terrors—as the LORD your God did for you in Egypt, before your eyes?"*

**Traditional Reading:**

Calvin: "He says that God 'took him a nation from the midst of another nation,' for by His incomparable power He rescued the descendants of Abraham, who, though dispersed through Egypt, and, as it were, enclosed in its bowels, were yet an obscure and ignoble part of a most famous nation; whereof no similar example is to be found." (https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/comment3/comm_vol03/htm/v.viii.htm)

Enduring Word cites Adam Clarke, who notes that "Moses enumerates seven different means used by the Almighty in effecting Israel's deliverance" in this verse. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-4/)

---

### v. 35: *"You were shown these things so that you would know that the LORD is God; there is no other besides Him."*

**Traditional Reading:**

Calvin: "He first says that God had so proved His divinity by miracles and prodigies, that the Israelites might know certainly that He was God. Whence, too, he concludes that He is the only God; for although God's holy name be torn in pieces by various opinions, whilst each one manufactures his own gods for himself, yet is it still sure that the power and dominion of God cannot be withdrawn from Him … Therefore the essence of the one God overthrows and annihilates all the other deities which we foolishly invent for ourselves." (https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/comment3/comm_vol03/htm/v.viii.htm)

Enduring Word: "Israel could know that the LORD was God, because of all the amazing things God did in the life of their nation. These included hearing the voice of God, trials, signs, wonders, war, and God's mighty hand. All these were given to testify to Israel that Yahweh—the LORD—is God." Merrill adds: "The nations of the earth might indeed have their mythic and epic traditions about the intervention of their gods on behalf of their ancestors or even themselves, but none of these can compare in the least to the act of delivering a disorganized, dispirited, militarily inexperienced horde of slaves from the dominion of the mightiest power on earth." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-4/)

---

### v. 36: *"He let you hear His voice from heaven to discipline you, and on earth He showed you His great fire, and you heard His words out of the fire."*

**Traditional Reading:**

Calvin reconciles the apparent tension of God's voice coming both from heaven and from the fire: "Moses simply means that the voice which flowed out of the fire into the people's ears was distinguished by plain indications which proved it to be heavenly." (https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/comment3/comm_vol03/htm/v.viii.htm)

The purpose is stated as "to discipline you" (or "instruct you") — God's self-revelation was pedagogical, designed to teach Israel who He is and how to fear Him.

---

### v. 37: *"Because He loved your fathers, He chose their descendants after them and brought you out of Egypt by His presence and great power."*

**Traditional Reading:**

Calvin draws out the doctrine of election: "Moses desires to shew that whatever good things God has conferred upon His people are gratuitous, by which circumstance he commends God's grace the more. He had said that by unusual favor this nation was taken from the midst of another; and he now adds that this was done on no other account but because God had embraced Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob with His love, and persevered in the same love towards their posterity." He stresses "that by the word 'love' is expressed that favor which springs of mere generosity, so as to exclude all worthiness in the person beloved." (https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/comment3/comm_vol03/htm/v.viii.htm)

Enduring Word concurs that this is an argument grounded in God's love for the patriarchs. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-4/)

**Where Traditions Differ:**

The Reformed tradition (Calvin) strongly emphasises unconditional election here: God's choice was "gratuitous," excluding "all worthiness in the person beloved." Arminian/Wesleyan traditions would affirm God's loving choice but typically emphasise that Israel was chosen for service and mission, with conditions of continued obedience attached, rather than an unconditional individual election to salvation. No specific Wesleyan/Methodist source was retrieved for this verse.

---

### v. 38: *"to drive out before you nations greater and mightier than you, and to bring you into their land and give it to you for your inheritance, as it is this day."*

**Traditional Reading:**

The language echoes the conquest narrative. The point is again God's power acting on behalf of an inferior people. Constable observes this verse is part of the "mounting crescendo of argument" that climaxes in v. 37-40, with "the articulation of God's motivation in His great redemptive and saving acts for Israel as being His love for them." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/deuteronomy-4.html)

---

### v. 39: *"Know therefore this day and take to heart that the LORD is God in heaven above and on the earth below; there is no other."*

**Traditional Reading:**

Calvin: "He again inculcates what we have lately spoken of, that the glory of the one true God was proved by the miracles, but he does so by way of exhortation. For he desires them carefully and attentively to consider what God had shewn them, because in so plain a matter there would be no excuse for error or ignorance." (https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/comment3/comm_vol03/htm/v.viii.htm)

Enduring Word: "This was a logical, rational response to hearing what Israel heard, seeing what they saw, and experiencing what they experienced." Trapp is quoted: "Where is God? Or rather, where is not God? He is higher than heaven, lower than hell, broader than the sea, longer than the earth…. He is nowhere, and yet everywhere; far from no place, and yet not contained in any place." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-4/)

---

### v. 40: *"Keep His statutes and commandments, which I am giving you today, so that you and your children after you may prosper, and that you may live long in the land that the LORD your God is giving you for all time."*

**Traditional Reading:**

Calvin: "The sum is, that they would be inexcusable if they did not obediently receive the Law, which they knew to have come from God; for they must needs be worse than stupid if the majesty of God, known and understood by so many proofs, did not awaken them to reverence." (https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/comment3/comm_vol03/htm/v.viii.htm)

Constable: "The best way to motivate people to obey God is to expound His character and conduct, as Moses did here. Note too that Moses appealed to the self-interest of the Israelites: 'that it may go well with you and with your children after you, and that you may live long on the land.'" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/deuteronomy-4.html)

Matthew Henry: "This argument he had begun with, ver. 1, *That ye may live, and go in and possess the land*; and this he concludes with, ver. 40, *That it may go well with thee, and with thy children after thee.* He reminds them that their prosperity would depend upon their piety." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/4-25.htm)

---

### vv. 41-43: Cities of Refuge East of the Jordan

*"Then Moses set aside three cities across the Jordan to the east to which a manslayer could flee after killing his neighbor unintentionally without prior malice. To save one's own life, he could flee to one of these cities: Bezer in the wilderness on the plateau belonging to the Reubenites, Ramoth in Gilead belonging to the Gadites, or Golan in Bashan belonging to the Manassites."*

**Traditional Reading:**

Calvin commends Moses' diligence: "God had destined … six cities for refuge … As to the three which He had appointed on the other side of Jordan, Moses records that he had faithfully performed what God had commanded. Hence it appears that, although he could not immediately comply with God's command to its full extent, still he did not wait until the three other cities could be added; but that, as far as circumstances permitted, he discharged his duty. Hence let us learn that, even when we cannot at once entirely carry out what God commands us to do, we are still to be by no means idle." (https://www.ccel.org/c/calvin/comment3/comm_vol06/htm/ii.xlvi.htm)

Constable notes the literary function: "The inclusion of this historical incident also serves a literary function. It provides a kind of intermission for the reader following the emotional climax at the end of the first address. It allows him or her to recover from its strong impact before the next long address begins." He also explains: "It may seem strange that Moses included the record of his appointment of Bezer, Ramoth, and Golan as the three cities of refuge … at this point in Deuteronomy. He probably did so because this important event took place after his first address and before he delivered his second speech." (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/deuteronomy/4-41.html)

**Reformed View (Ligonier):**

Ligonier draws out the gospel typology: "God showed grace without compromising the value of human life when He provided the cities of refuge for those who committed manslaughter." The provision required an initial hearing before the elders; admission was not automatic. "Death was still required to pay for the killing of the innocent person, for manslaughter is a form of killing … But as the killing is unintentional in manslaughter, grace was shown to the killer. The high priest's death was substituted, which points finally to Jesus, the perfect High Priest, who died for all the sins of His people (Heb. 2:17)." (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/designating-cities-of-refuge)

The Ligonier devotional also notes: "In the ancient world, feuds could be a part of everyday life. If you killed my sister, even by accident, I might kill your brother. Then your family might kill my cousin, and so on. In setting up places for those who committed manslaughter to flee and find legal protection, a powerful check was placed upon blood-feuding and innocent life was protected from harm." (https://www.ligonier.org/learn/devotionals/dividing-land/)

Gill notes the purpose: "that the slayer might flee thither, which should kill his neighbor unawares, and hated him not in times past; and that, fleeing unto one of these cities, he might live." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/4.htm)

---

### vv. 44-45: *"This is the law that Moses set before the Israelites. These are the testimonies, statutes, and ordinances that Moses proclaimed to them after they had come out of Egypt."*

**Traditional Reading:**

Ellicott calls these verses "an introduction to the second discourse, which occupies the larger portion of the book—from Deuteronomy 5:1 to the end of Deuteronomy 26. There is no real break between." He notes that unlike the introduction in Deuteronomy 1:1, "There is no intimation that this portion of Deuteronomy was a repetition of what had been delivered between Sinai and Kadesh-barnea. What follows is said to have been spoken in the land of Sihon and Og, after the conquest by Israel." Ellicott acknowledges the possibility that "The whole passage (Deuteronomy 4:44-49) may be editorial, and added by Joshua in Canaan. But there is no necessity for this view." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/4.htm)

Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: "This is a preface to the rehearsal of the law, which, with the addition of various explanatory circumstances, the following chapters contain." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/deuteronomy/4.htm)

Gill: "These are the testimonies, and the statutes, and the judgments … The laws, moral, ceremonial, and judicial, delivered in the following chapters; which are renewed, repeated." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/4.htm)

---

### vv. 46-49: Historical and Geographical Setting

*"while they were in the valley across the Jordan facing Beth-peor in the land of Sihon king of the Amorites … extending from Aroer on the rim of the Arnon Valley as far as Mount Siyon (that is, Hermon), including all the Arabah on the east side of the Jordan and as far as the Sea of the Arabah, below the slopes of Pisgah."*

**Traditional Reading:**

Keil & Delitzsch: "'In the valley,' as in Deuteronomy 3:29. 'In the land of Sihon,' and therefore already upon ground which the Lord had given them for a possession. The importance of this possession as the first-fruit and pledge of the fulfilment of the further promises of God, led Moses to mention again, though briefly, the defeat of the two kings of the Amorites, together with the conquest of their land, just as he had done before in Deuteronomy 2:32-36 and Deuteronomy 3:1-17." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/4-49.htm)

The location is significant: Israel is encamped in the Jordan Valley opposite Beth-peor—the very place where the Baal-Peor incident occurred (Numbers 25). This geographical reminder reinforces the warnings against idolatry that dominate the chapter. "Beth-peor" means "house of Peor," referring to the Moabite god.

Mount Siyon is identified as Mount Hermon. The "Sea of the Arabah" is the Dead Sea. "Below the slopes of Pisgah" refers to the mountain from which Moses would later view the Promised Land (Deuteronomy 34:1).

---

## Summary of Where Protestant Traditions Differ

1. **Dispensational vs. Non-Dispensational on vv. 29-31:** Dispensational teachers (MacArthur, Precept Austin) read the "latter days" as end-times tribulation and national Israel's future conversion before a literal millennium. Reformed covenant theologians (Gospel Coalition, Ligonier) typically see these restoration promises fulfilled in Christ and applied spiritually to the church, without requiring a distinct future for national Israel.

2. **Reformed vs. Arminian on v. 37:** Calvin emphasises unconditional election — God's love for the fathers excluded "all worthiness in the person beloved." Wesleyan/Arminian traditions (not found in the searched pages) would underscore human responsibility and conditional covenant faithfulness alongside divine love.

3. **Baptist (Spurgeon) on vv. 29-31:** Spurgeon applies the call to "seek the LORD" universally to all sinners, treating the passage as an evangelistic invitation — a characteristic Baptist emphasis on personal conversion and the "whosoever will" of the gospel.

4. **Critical Scholarship (Cambridge Bible):** Notes that some scholars view vv. 29-31 as a "later exilic insertion" and vv. 44-49 as possibly "editorial." These source-critical observations are not embraced in traditional Protestant teaching but appear in academic commentaries.
